articles.text: The Montana brand book is now being circulated and is the best one of the kind ever published. It reflects great credit on its compilers and will be of great value to the stockmen of the Montana Stockgrowers' Association.
articles.summary: Praise for the newly circulated Montana brand book.

articles.text: Hough & Dustin of Miles City, expect to open their slaughter-house to-morrow. They have facilities for killing from seventy-five to a hundred head a day. Their limited cold storage capacity will confine them to about fifty a day however.
articles.summary: Hough & Dustin of Miles City expect to open their slaughter-house the next day.

articles.text: War has begun on rates between St. Paul and Chicago. The rate some time ago was $14.25, which has now been rereduced to $3.00. This is owing to the fact that the Northwestern and Milwaukee roads have put on fast trains, making better time than is possible for the Rock Island which has 130 miles longer haul. To meet the reduced time, the Rock Island has cut rates, which are now met by the other roads. The fight will probably be a long one, as the other roads will combine to freeze out the Rock Island. This road is a stayer though and we look for it to secure its fair share of the travel.
articles.summary: A rate war between St. Paul and Chicago has cut the fare from $14.25 to $3.00.

articles.text: Stories of skill in the use of the lariat are numerous but one told by Harry Bennett as seen by him on his return from McGinness, makes a big bid for first place. Harry struck a round-up party north of the Yellowstone and camped with a wagon run by Jess Reeves, well known as one of the best cow-punchers in the Yellowstone country. In the morning as they started out, Jess jumped up a jack-rabbit. Hastily grabbing his rope he threw it and heeled Mr. J. Rabbitt as neatly as the operation was ever performed on a steer. Of course there was considerable luck in the throw, but all who know Jess, swear that he could do it if any one could.
articles.summary: Harry Bennett tells of cow-puncher Jess Reeves roping a jack-rabbit by the heels north of the Yellowstone.

articles.text: The rains of Friday, Saturday, Sunday and Monday have put an entirely different complexion on the feed question. In themselves, they guarantee that there will be sufficient grass for grazing purposes, but the hay question is still far from being settled. The grass has undoubtedly taken a fresh start, but whether there will be enough for hay is doubtful. In some favored localities we have a good crop, but these spots are less than an acre generally in extent and are widely scattered. These facts bring forward more prominently than before, the question of raising tame hay for ranch use. As we have often said, there is no avoiding this issue. There are getting to be so many cattle in the Bad Lands, that the grass is not given a chance to attain its full growth. Hereafter, even a moderately dry season will show a shortage or total lack of hay. This summer and coming winter are good times for our cowmen to carefully ponder this subject.
articles.summary: Four days of rain have assured grazing grass, but the editor warns the overstocked Bad Lands need tame hay.

articles.text: The St. Paul stock-market scheme seems to be entirely a thing of the past. The Cow Boy did not see at the time the plan was first brought up how it could possibly be a success and stated fully its reasons for its belief. The real origin of the whole plan, we firmly believe, was a land speculation. Several interested persons had a block of land that would bring a good price for stock yards and wished to make a sale. Hence their solicitous care to relieve the stockmen from the Chicago monoply. But there happened to be other blocks of land near St. Paul, with owners equally anxious to make sales and as the matter was getting to a question of bidding and a consequent reduction in price, the original movers are beginning to think that they will let the cattlemen struggle on a while longer. Humanity is all right as long as it is a money-making scheme but it lacks lots of being popular when it is not.
articles.summary: The editor declares the St. Paul stock-market scheme dead and calls it a land speculation.

articles.text: It is seldom that we sympathize with a movement in which private citizens take the law in their own hands to punish offenders, but we wish to be put on record right here as approving in every way with the action of the citizens of Mingusville in flogging a sneak-thief there recently. It appears that the thief had brought in some cattle to deliver and had stolen some small articles, such as a slicker, quirt, chapps &c., intending to clear out of the country with them. He was detected and according to the article from our Mingusville correspondent, published in another column, it must be extremely uncomfortable for the "quirtee" to sit down even now. Had the man been arrested and taken to Glendive, he would have been fined a small amount and then turned loose. As it is, he will have such a wholesmoe remembrance of the result of his thieving, that he will propably not engage in it again. The effect on other offenders will also be far greater than if the thief had been arrested and we can almost guarantee Mingusville immunity from petty thieving for some time to come. Small frontier towns are always great losers from the operations of this kind of robbers and nothing will so arouse public spirit against them as summary punishment of this kind.
articles.summary: The editor approves of Mingusville citizens flogging a sneak-thief rather than taking him to court at Glendive.

articles.text: A cattle and sneak-thief named James Harrison alias "Buckskin" has been arrested south of Mandan. He will doubtless get the full benefit of the law. Last fall he butchered and sold in Bismarck, six animals belonging to different owners.
articles.summary: Cattle thief James Harrison, alias 'Buckskin', has been arrested south of Mandan.

articles.text: The New Mexico Stock Grower is urging the advisability of digging wells for the cowmen of New Mexico. Provided the Sioux reservation is opened, it will need no urging for cowmen to sink artisian wells all through the old limits of the reservation. It is destined to become a great cow country.
articles.summary: If the Sioux reservation is opened, cowmen will sink artesian wells there.

articles.text: The cattle are in far better condition than could possibly be expected. At least thirty per cent. of four-year-old steers would now make prime beef and in three weeks this per cent. will be increased to eighty. Instead of the beef being later this year than last, it will probably be two weeks earlier.
articles.summary: Cattle are in better condition than expected and beef will likely be two weeks earlier than last year.

articles.text: Outfits will be immediately made up both north and south of the track to round-up all the country east, going as far as the Missouri river if necessary. They will probably start inside of a week. The country to be rounded up is an immense one, extending from the Killdeer Mts. to Cave Hills and from the Bad Lands to the Missouri; in round numbers about 170 miles square.
articles.summary: Outfits are forming north and south of the track to round up the country east to the Missouri.

articles.text: The Chicago stock market shows a gain in prime cattle and a drop to $1.00 per 100 for scalawags. Compared with a year ago, Texas cattle are fifty cents lower, owing to their inferior condition. There were about 7,000 of these cattle on the market during last week, cows and bulls selling at $2.25 @ 3.25 and steers at $[3?].80 @ 4.90. Grass Texans generally sold under $3.40. In Liverpool, the best American dressed beef sells at 13½c. per lb.
articles.summary: Chicago market report on prime cattle and Texas cattle prices.

articles.text: M. Wadsworth, of the Bad Lands cattle Co., has experimented with several different kinds of grasses this year. Alfalfa and millet bid fair to do the best, but our recent dry spell killed nearly all of the latter. It started well and with all the way from twelve to twenty stalks to the seed but as stated, was badly nipped by the drouth. The alfalfa, on the other hand has done splendidly from the start. It started out well and has kept green and growing through the dry weather that even browned the native grasses. Of course the experiment is not yet conclusive, but it goes a long way to prove all that the advocates of alfalfa have claimed for it. As before stated in the Cow Boy, in at least ten cases throughout Dakota, alfalfa has been a gratifying success. In not one case coming to our notice has it proved a failure. This season will finally decide the matter, as all over Dakota, alfalfa is now growing and we certainly expect that it will prove to be all that is claimed for it; the forage plant par excellence.
articles.summary: M. Wadsworth of the Bad Lands Cattle Co. reports alfalfa thriving through the drouth while his millet failed.

articles.text: To-day is the last day of the round-up, the work being finished at Sully creek ranch. Only twenty-two days were consumed in the work; a shorter time than any Bad Lands round-up has yet taken. The boys all worked well and the only rest they had was one day off on account of a pouring rain. Five hours' sleep was a rarity, the average being nearer four. On several occasions dinner, or at least the second meal of the day, was served at seven o'clock in the morning. There was not a moment's waste time except at meals and working hours were from seventeen to eighteen hours a day. The most of the boys, having so little use for their beds, wanted to trade them off for lanterns. At least they said they did. It has long been recognized as an impossible task to make a perfectly clean round-up of the Bad Lands. Cattle will hide away in the dense brush of out-of-the-way coolies, especially cows with calves. The last week there has been further difficulty that water was abundant everywhere and very few cattle came down on the river and creek bottoms. The figures on the calf crop are as hard to obtain as ever. The round-up has not shown a present increase of over thirty per cent. When the fact is taken into consideration that there may have been ten per cent. of the calves missed and that the fall round-up will show as great or greater per cent. than did this round-up, the result is more encouraging than any the Bad Lands has yet had. Steers are generally in very good condition, a large per cent. being now fit for beef. Taking into consideration the amount of hard riding done, the horses are in far better condition than could be expected. As a whole, the work done was very satisfactory.
articles.summary: The spring Bad Lands round-up ends at Sully creek ranch after a record twenty-two days, with a calf increase of about thirty per cent.

articles.text: S. E. Grindall, deputy-sheriff at Mingusville, was in town last Thursday. He reports cattle as doing well in the Beaver valley, but that the grass needed rain as much as it did here.

articles.text: H. S. Boice has gone to the Northwest Territory, to look up the stock ranges there. The Canadian government is offering great inducements to Amerian cowmen to range their cattle there. Long time, low-rate leases and free entry into Canada are the bait used to catch them.
articles.summary: H. S. Boice has gone to the Canadian Northwest Territory to look at stock ranges.

articles.text: Harry Bennett returned Saturday from his trip to Fort McGinness after Johnny Goodall's horses. He found them, eight in all, about sixty miles west of the fort. On his return, he picked up one belonging to Wall Osterhaut, near Miles City. Harry reports that cattle are doing better in the Bad Lands than they are further west, owing to the superior feed. He made the round trip of over 1,000 miles in twenty-one days. Going, he only had one horse to ride and returning, he drove eight and nine horses. Altogether it is good enough time to go on record.
articles.summary: Harry Bennett returned from Fort McGinness with Johnny Goodall's eight horses after a 1,000-mile, 21-day round trip.

articles.text: A man named Landrum from Glendive, borrowed a saddle and outfit here recently from Dan. McKenzie and E. G. Paddock and started to Mingusville. He sent word that he had shipped them back but it was learned that he had taken them to Glendive. Mr. Paddock went up to Glendive and found Landrum there with the goods and after a vigorous use of the King's English, brought them back with him. No criminal case can be made out against Landrum, or he wonld propably suffer for his action.
articles.summary: E. G. Paddock recovered a saddle and outfit that a Glendive man named Landrum had borrowed and carried off.

articles.text: Sheriff Sebastian of Stark county and L. N. Cary of Mandan, returned Monday from locating the scene of the murder of Dode Straugh in the year of 1883, by Dave Lee. It was a point of dispute whether the murder was committed in Daketa or Montana. Messrs. Sebastian and Cary surveyed the ground and found that the scene of the murder was in Dakota, five miles from Montana, on the line between Ewing and Bowman counties, at the mouth of the Box Elder, where the Hash knife cattle company now have their home ranch. Straugh was a buffalo hunter from Spearfish and Lee was a cow-boy. In a dispute over a game of cards, the murder was committed. There is said to be abundant evidence to convict Lee.
articles.summary: Sheriff Sebastian and L. N. Cary established that Dave Lee's 1883 killing of Dode Straugh took place in Dakota, at the mouth of the Box Elder.

articles.headline: Communication.
articles.text:
Mingusville Mont., June 14, 1886.
Editor Bad Lands Cow Boy:—

Mingusville takes the cake in the way of reform movement. Our patient but long-suffering people have tired of the too effective work of the sneak-thief and at least one of that fraternity will ever remember us. This one made himself very busy taking quirts, slickers, leggins etc., but was caught and after being compelled to deliver each article to its rightful owner was taken to the platform at the depot, bent over a convenient spool of barbed fence wire and given an energetic application of five lashes each by some half a dozen healthy men. We understand that blood was drawn. Perhaps the thief was too severely punished, yet he deserved some attention and received it in a way much less expensive than by arrest and law proceedings and doubtless more effectively; without it costing the tax payers of Dawson county a cent. There are people here who seemingly propose to make sneak-theiving much more of a rarity than it has been.

X
articles.summary: A Mingusville correspondent describes citizens flogging a sneak-thief at the depot platform.

articles.text:
Sheriff's Sale.
[First publication May 6.]

Ter. of Dakota, County of Morton, To which county Billings county is attached for judicial purposes. } SS.

Notice is hereby given that by virtue of a judgment and decree in foreclosure, rendered and given by the District Court of the sixth judicial district, in and for the county of Morton, (to which county Billings county is attached for judicial purposes,) and Territory of Dakota, and filed in the office of said court, on the 23rd. day of April, A. D. 1886, in an action wherein the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company is plaintiff and John Kiefer and Mary J. Kiefer are defendants, in favor of said plaintiff, and against said defendant, for the sum of One thousand three hundred and twenty-seven dollars and fifty-three cents ($1,327.53,) the principal and interest secured by a certain mortgage, given by John Kiefer and Mary J. Kiefer, his wife, to the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company, together with interest thereon from April 10th., A. D. 1886, the date of said decree and also the cost of said plaintiff, taxed at the sum of ninety-one dollars and thirty-five cents, ($91.35,) which judgment and decree directed the sale by me of the real estate hereinafter described, to satisfy the amount of said judgment, with interest thereon, and costs and expenses of said sale, or so much thereof as the proceeds of such sale, applicable thereto, will satisfy, and by virtue of a writ issued out of the office of the Clerk of said court, in and for said county of Morton, to which county, Billings county is attached for judicial purposes, and under the seal of said court, directing me to sell said real property, pursuant to said judgment and decree,

I, George W. Harmon, Sheriff of said Morton county and the person appointed by said court to make said sale, will sell the hereinafter described real estate to the highest bidder, for cash, at public auction, at the front door of the Court House in the city of Mandan, in the county of Morton, (to which county Billings county is attached for judicial purposes,) and Territory of Dakota, on the 17th day of June, A. D. 1886, at two o'clock, P. M., of that day, to satisfy said judgment, interest and costs, and the costs and expenses of such sale, or so much thereof as the proceeds of such sale, applicable thereto, will satisfy.

The premises to be sold as aforesaid, pursuant to said judgment and decree, and to said writ, and to this notice, are described in said judgment, decree and writ, as follows, to-wit:

All those tracts or parcels of land lying and being in the County of Billings, and Territory of Dakota, described as follows:

Lots number Thirteen (13) and Fourteen (14) in Block number nine (9,) as laid down and designated on the plat of the town of Medora, Billings county, D. T., as the same is recorded in the office of Register of Deeds of Morton county, D. T., to which County Billings county, which is unorganized, is attached for judicial purposes.

Dated at Mandan, Dakota. April 29, A. D., 1886.
George W. Harmon, Sheriff, Morton County, Dakota.
Edward S. Allen, Plaintiff's Att'y.
